children.name: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance
children.blurb: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance is the structured review of how an organisation's finance function actually uses artificial intelligence, covering the tools in play, the data feeding them, the controls around them and the evidence trail they leave.

children.name: Keeping Financial Data Out of Public Models
children.blurb: Keeping financial data out of public models covers the controls that stop ledgers, payroll files, deal documents and client records from being pasted into consumer chatbots or uploaded to third party AI services.

children.name: Model Risk and Bias Testing
children.blurb: Model risk and bias testing covers the checks an organisation runs on a model before and after it goes into use, to see whether it produces wrong, unstable or unfairly skewed outputs.

children.name: Mapping Financial AI to the Rules
children.blurb: Mapping financial AI to the rules is the work of connecting each model, tool or automated decision in a finance function to the specific regulation, accounting standard or supervisory expectation that governs it.

children.name: Local and Air-Gapped Deployment
children.blurb: Local and air-gapped deployment covers AI systems that run on hardware the organisation controls, with no dependency on an outside network.

sections.body: This section covers the controls, checks and deployment choices that sit between an accounting function and the AI tools it wants to use. In practice the work is unglamorous: reviewing which systems touch client ledgers, testing whether a model produces different answers for similar borrowers, and writing down who approved what. Finance teams are doing this now because auditors and regulators ask for evidence, not intentions. The field borrows from IT security, model risk management and compliance, and it is usually run by a mix of finance, risk and technology staff rather than by data scientists alone.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are reasonably settled. Access control, encryption and vendor review are mature practices that most firms already apply to other software, and air-gapped deployment is a known option for sensitive workloads. What is not solved is measurement. Bias testing in credit and fraud models still depends on choices about which groups to compare and what counts as a meaningful gap, and those choices are contested. Mapping rules is also unsettled because obligations arrive from several directions at once, and this site tracks 229 compliance and regulation pages alongside 150 active AI lawsuits, which shows how much is still being argued rather than decided. The honest limit is that no test proves a model is safe, only that it passed the checks someone defined.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader starting from scratch should begin with The AI Enablement Audit in Finance, which sets out how a firm takes stock of what it is already using and who owns it. Keeping Financial Data Out of Public Models follows naturally, since leakage is the risk that turns a routine pilot into an incident, and it deals with prompts, retention and vendor terms. Model Risk and Bias Testing goes deeper into the statistical side, covering validation, monitoring and the difficulty of defining fairness. Mapping Financial AI to the Rules connects that internal work to external obligations, and Local and Air-Gapped Deployment is the practical end of the chain, describing how to run models where data cannot leave the building. Read together they form a sequence from inventory to containment to testing to justification to architecture.
